candidate_claims.claim_verbatim: Think on average, we are 30 degrees cooler than Texas, which, when you look at your PUE math, could save a one-gigawatt plant upwards of $150 million a year
candidate_claims.why_load_bearing: Cooling/PUE savings is Dunleavy's most-repeated QUANTITATIVE selling point to hyperscalers (Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, DigitalBridge). A specific $150M/yr figure anchors total-cost-of-ownership expectations for capital allocators evaluating Alaska siting. If cooling is marginal and Alaska power is the most expensive in the nation, the TCO math inverts.

prelim_counter_evidence.fact: UAF Alaska Center for Energy and Power: 'cooling costs typically represent 5% or less of ongoing operations and maintenance costs' for hyperscale data centers, and 'the commercial electricity rate in Alaska is much higher than any other U.S. state.'

Large commercial users on Chugach's Southcentral system pay roughly 14 to 17 cents per kWh vs ~6.12c Texas, ~8.99c Virginia, ~6.61c Washington (2024 EIA). The power-cost penalty dwarfs any cooling-derived PUE savings.
AI GPU-dense workloads typically require liquid cooling regardless of ambient temperature, limiting the free-air advantage.

candidate_claims.recurrence_note: Recurs in Dunleavy's CES 2026 panel, Data Center World April 2026, Data Center Knowledge Oct 2025; McCabe's April ADN op-ed ('an advantage for cooling'); Stak Energy project docs (12F average temp as 'design advantage'). Single most-repeated supporting claim across the data-center pitch.
candidate_claims.repeat_risk: Data-center-adjacent theme but a DISTINCT claim: cooling/PUE economics, not anchor-tenant/gas-supply (06-09) or land leases (06-07). Not previously corrected.

candidate_claims.claim_verbatim: With a cost per flight hour about one-tenth that of an F-35, MALE UAS would be a sustainable way to expand air defense capacity across America's arctic approaches.

asserters.name: Bryan Clark
asserters.title_or_org: Senior Fellow & Director, Center for Defense Concepts and Technology, Hudson Institute
asserters.outlet: Hudson Institute / House Homeland Security testimony

candidate_claims.why_load_bearing: Named analyst congressional testimony shapes DoD acquisition priorities and Alaska-based contractor investment. Positioning MALE UAS as the cheap AI-enabled Arctic air-defense solution redirects procurement dollars toward a technology class whose performance degrades sharply in Alaska cold.

prelim_counter_evidence.fact: Army 11th Airborne UAS experiments at Joint Pacific Alaskan Range Complex (Nov 2025): drone batteries deliver only 25-50% of advertised flight time in extreme cold; devices crack at -40F; no small drone found that 'consistently fly[s] in more than light rain or dry snow.' Tablets crack 'around negative 40.'

CEPA Dec 2025: 'In a recent German winter exercise, batteries of US military small quadcopters delivered only 25-50% of advertised flight time,' and 'AI-enabled swarming can reduce manpower but adds extra cost, forcing quantity-versus-quality tradeoffs.'

candidate_claims.recurrence_note: Near-consensus among defense trade/think-tanks: CEPA (MQ-9B SeaGuardian for Arctic), FPRI Nov 2025 ('future of human presence in the Arctic might be uncrewed'), Air & Space Forces Magazine Nov 2025, NATO in the North 2025 exercise.
candidate_claims.repeat_risk: FRESH defense angle; not in any of the last 6 corrections. Fully outside saturated themes.

candidate_claims.claim_verbatim: We are going to embark upon a very robust fiber process so Alaska can become the center of data transmission for three continents.
candidate_claims.why_load_bearing: Anchors the geographic/latency case for hundred-million-dollar Alaska data-center investment. If fiber is unbuilt/unfunded, early movers bear stranded-asset risk.

prelim_counter_evidence.fact: Alaska connects to CONUS via only two undersea cables; ACEP (2024) identifies fiber connectivity as 'the biggest challenge' and a 2024 cable cut showed statewide vulnerability. Dunleavy's own words ('we are going to embark') concede the process hasn't begun; 2031 target.

candidate_claims.recurrence_note: Asserted by Dunleavy at two trade events; echoed by Keith Dobson (INVITE Networks) in Must Read Alaska and Far North Fiber promo materials.
candidate_claims.repeat_risk: Connectivity theme overlaps 06-06 (Arctic satellites) and 06-13 (broadband). Moderate repeat risk.

candidate_claims.claim_verbatim: Alaska has done none of that. No comprehensive policy, no clear direction, no coordinated strategy.
candidate_claims.why_load_bearing: Drives capital-allocation skepticism and calls for state incentive packages / task forces. If decision-makers accept Alaska is a policy blank slate, they may defer investment.

prelim_counter_evidence.fact: 34th Legislature established a Joint Legislative Task Force on AI (HCR 3); DEED published AI guidelines for districts Oct 2025; Dunleavy AO 359/360 directs agencies to use AI. Not a void, though arguably thin.

candidate_claims.recurrence_note: Blank-slate frame recurs in ADN opinion section through Q1-Q2 2026.
candidate_claims.repeat_risk: Fresh, but rebuttal is contestable (task force reportedly stalled); 'no strategy' partly true. Weaker for a clean correction.

candidate_claims.claim_verbatim: AI protocols could lead to improved cost-effectiveness and faster turnaround times for video review.

asserters.name: Caren Brady
asserters.title_or_org: Senior Program Manager, Pacific States Marine Fisheries Commission

candidate_claims.why_load_bearing: Alaska halibut/sablefish fleet face federally mandated observer-coverage costs. The AI-EM claim shapes whether vessel owners and ALFA invest in the tech ($485K grant) as a compliance solution.

prelim_counter_evidence.fact: National Fisherman (2023): at-sea AI species-ID still 'not yet fully operational and on the market'; data uploads only after vessels return, not real time; real-time bycatch AI 'a year or two away.'

candidate_claims.recurrence_note: Echoed in ALFA membership comms and NOAA Fisheries program docs.
candidate_claims.repeat_risk: Fresh theme, but low circulation (2) and counter-evidence is 2023/dated. Weaker on rebuttable-from-current-primary-evidence.

candidate_claims.claim_verbatim: Artificial Intelligence has the potential to help the Department of Energy and our National Labs accomplish enormous challenges in the fields of science and technology, as well as offer capabilities to streamline permitting for large-scale energy and critical mineral projects in Alaska.
candidate_claims.why_load_bearing: Critical-minerals and energy developers count on AI-accelerated federal permitting. If DOE AI permitting tools are nascent/undeployed, the expectation is ungrounded.

prelim_counter_evidence.fact: DOE AI Act (S.4859, July 2024) not enacted standalone; no public DOE deployment of Alaska-specific AI permitting tools through June 2026. Dunleavy AO 360 frames AI permitting as future directive, not operational system.

candidate_claims.recurrence_note: Continues to circulate in critical-minerals coverage 2025-2026.
candidate_claims.repeat_risk: Fresh; but claim is from 2024 and hedged ('has the potential'), making it harder to call wrong vs. merely aspirational.
